analysis.one_liner: Lets local regulators cap basic cable rates and sets service standards where cable faces no competition.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote, but its proposals were carried into a successor cable bill, H.R. 4850, that became the Cable Act of 1992 over President Bush's veto.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 1984 cable law stripped local governments of rate-setting power, basic cable prices rose far faster than inflation — about 56 to 61 percent between 1986 and 1991, versus 17.9 percent for the Consumer Price Index — while roughly 97 percent of franchises were deregulated. This bill would give the FCC or local franchising authorities the power to regulate basic cable rates wherever a cable system faces no effective competition, set national customer service and signal quality standards, and bar cable operators from favoring programmers they own. It would also require satellite programmers to keep serving home dish owners and limit how much of the market one cable company can control.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 54 million households subscribing to cable at the time, who would get a ceiling on basic-cable rates, enforceable customer service and picture quality standards, and protection from discrimination in rates and programming access. C-band home satellite dish owners would benefit from required continued access to satellite programming, and independent programmers not owned by cable companies would gain the right to fair carriage terms.

how_it_helps.text: Cable rates rose 56 to 61 percent between December 1986 and April 1991 while the Consumer Price Index rose 17.9 percent, and a Justice Department economist estimated 45 to 50 percent of those increases came from market power — the bill would let the FCC or certified local authorities regulate basic rates wherever a cable system lacks effective competition.

It requires FCC customer service standards covering office hours, installation and repair response times, billing and refund practices, and complaint procedures, and lets state and local governments impose stricter standards.

It bars cable operators from unreasonably discriminating among subscribers and bars national programmers from refusing to deal with or price-discriminating against competing distributors, including home satellite services.

It directs the FCC to set limits on how many subscribers one person's cable systems may reach and how many channels a cable operator's affiliated programmers may occupy, aimed at the industry's concentrated and vertically integrated structure.

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, who would give up unregulated pricing power on their monopoly basic tiers and face ownership limits, annual financial reporting to regulators, service quality mandates, and duties to deal with independent programmers and distributors. Vertically integrated programmers partly owned by cable companies would lose their ability to secure exclusive or favored carriage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable operators and their affiliated programmers

drawbacks.text: Regulated rates based on cost reviews and annual financial reporting add compliance costs and could reduce cable operators' incentive to invest in upgrading systems, a trade-off supporters accepted in exchange for protecting subscribers from monopoly pricing.

The bill shields local franchising authorities from money damages in court over their cable decisions, limiting most relief to injunctions — a protection for local governments folded into a consumer bill.

The 'effective competition' test is detailed and litigable: cable operators can petition to challenge a franchising authority's rate regulation, and defining competition through two unaffiliated distributors reaching most households leaves room for disputes over when regulation ends.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the trade-off was heavily one-sided: cable was a local monopoly whose prices rose three to four times the inflation rate after rate regulation was stripped away, and the bill's costs fall mainly on industry profits and compliance spending. The genuine risks — dampened investment and regulatory disputes over when competition exists — are real but modest compared with the pricing power being curbed.

outcome.mechanism: It never got a vote: after being referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Telecommunications and Finance Subcommittee, it sat there until July 1992, when the record noted further action was in H.R. 4850 — the successor bill that became the Cable Act of 1992 and was enacted over President George H.W. Bush's veto.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced October 15, 1991 by Rep. Dennis Eckart with Reps. Cooper and Shays as original cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
On October 25, 1991 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, where no further action was taken.

The bill's findings document that rates for basic cable rose 56 to 61 percent between December 1986 and April 1991 while the Consumer Price Index rose 17.9 percent, and that about 97 percent of cable franchises had been deregulated since December 1986.
On July 23, 1992 the action history recorded 'For Further Action See H.R. 4850,' meaning the bill's substance was carried into a successor cable bill rather than advancing on its own.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable subscribers came out ahead in the end: the bill's core proposals were enacted through the successor Cable Act of 1992, passed over President George H.W. Bush's veto, reversing roughly six years of deregulated monopoly pricing for cable operators. This particular bill itself benefited no one but did not need to — its substance lived on.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable subscribers, via the 1992 Cable Act

for.name: Rep. Dennis E. Eckart
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cable Consumer Protection Act of 1991 and gathered additional sponsors.

for.name: 10 House cosponsors
for.role: Original and added cosponsors (8 Democrats, 2 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Reps. Cooper and Shays.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, which never reported it back, so it never reached the House floor for a vote.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed cable rate regulation and vetoed the successor cable bill (H.R. 4850), though Congress overrode the veto.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape is unrecorded; sponsorship was bipartisan but Democratic-leaning, with 8 of 10 cosponsors Democrats and 2 Republicans, and the referral committee was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill strips back their deregulated pricing power on basic service, imposes service quality and reporting duties, and caps how many subscribers and channels they can control. Their interest ran against the subscribers whose prices had risen 56 to 61 percent since deregulation.

Programmers affiliated with cable operators would lose favored carriage, exclusive distributorships, and the ability to demand financial interests as a condition of carriage. Independent programmers would gain the access they were being denied.

industries.industry: Satellite programming carriers and C-band dish industry
industries.note: The bill forces programmers and fixed-service satellite carriers to keep serving C-band home dish owners and deal fairly with distributors, helping dish owners and the home satellite market at the expense of programmers' pricing discretion.

FCC compatibility standards would require cable-ready technology in TVs and VCRs and retail availability of converters, adding manufacturing requirements but benefiting subscribers and retail sellers of equipment.
